summary: Describes extensions to IS-IS to support optimal routing within a two-level domain by distributing prefixes domain-wide. It is informational and was later replaced by RFC 5302.

plainLanguage.summary: Big networks are split into areas. This lets routes be shared across areas so traffic takes the best path.

questions: how does is-is handle inter-area routing
subtitle: Routing information sharing across network hierarchy layers.

tldr.problem: Large networks divided into areas for scalability lose information when summarizing prefixes, leading to suboptimal routing choices, especially for exit selection and metric advertisement.
tldr.mechanism: IS-IS extends level 1 and level 2 routers to distribute specific IP prefixes across hierarchy levels, using an up/down bit to prevent routing loops.
tldr.outcome: Networks can trade some scalability for better route optimality and more accurate metric information across areas. This was later replaced by RFC 5302.

today: RFC 2966 is an Informational RFC published in October 2000 and is now obsoleted by RFC 5302, which provides a more comprehensive treatment of IS-IS extensions.

sections.title: The Two-Level IS-IS Architecture
sections.content:
IS-IS divides routing domains into level 1 (area-local) and level 2 (backbone) routers to scale efficiently. Level 1 routers exchange information within their area; level 2 routers link areas together. RFC 1195 defines this boundary: routers typically summarize all area prefixes into a single advertisement sent to the backbone.

This summarization limits routing quality. If a level 2 router wants to reach a destination inside a level 1 area, it cannot distinguish between two equally good exit points within that area because it only knows the summarized prefix, not the internal topology.
sections.plainLanguage: Big networks are organized in areas. Normally, each area sends one summary of all its addresses to the backbone. This summary loses detail about the best route.

sections.title: Why Share More Detailed Routing Information
sections.content:
Route optimality: Without detailed prefix information, routers compute routes to destinations based on less complete information, often choosing a suboptimal path. Level 2 routers may select an entry point to an area that is not the best path when viewed from inside that area.

BGP route selection: When a router learns multiple paths to external destinations via BGP, it selects one based partly on the IGP (Interior Gateway Protocol) cost to the BGP next hop. Without detailed IGP metrics across areas, this shortest exit routing cannot work well. Multi-exit discriminators (MEDs): Networks commonly use the IGP metric as part of the BGP MED value to signal optimal entry points. Without domain-wide prefix distribution, this metric does not reflect true end-to-end distance.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three reasons: finding the fastest route, picking the cheapest exit point for external traffic, and advertising costs accurately to neighbors.

sections.title: The Up/Down Bit and Prefix Leaking
sections.content:
The core mechanism uses a single bit in the TLV 128/130 metric field, the up/down bit, to track the direction of prefix advertisement. Level 1L2 routers set this bit to one when advertising level 2 routes into level 1. This signals that these prefixes came from level 2 and must never be advertised back into level 2.

Without this protection, a level 1L2 router could learn a route that originated in level 2, was summarized into level 1, then learn it again from another level 1L2 router and advertise it back to level 2, creating a loop or suboptimal path. The up/down bit ensures that routing loops and path oscillations do not form.
sections.plainLanguage: A single bit marks whether a route came down from the backbone or came up from an area. If it came down, the area router never sends it back up, preventing loops.

sections.title: Scalability and Backward Compatibility
sections.content:
Domain-wide prefix distribution increases the number of prefixes throughout the network, growing memory, transmission, and computation costs. This is the cost of optimality: the trade-off is explicit and expected.

The extension maintains partial backward compatibility. Routers that do not understand the up/down bit will treat level 2 routes leaking into level 1 as normal level 1 routes and may advertise them back into level 2, creating loops. For this reason, all level 1L2 routers in an area must support the new up/down bit if the feature is enabled. The RFC recommends that implementations disable this feature by default and require explicit configuration.
sections.plainLanguage: More details means more data stored and sent. Older routers that do not know the up/down bit could break things, so administrators must configure it carefully.

sections.title: Standards and Related Work
sections.content: The document builds on RFC 1195, which defines IS-IS extensions for IPv4 and the original two-level hierarchy. RFC 1142 is the ISO standard republication. The RFC also compares with future work on IS-IS traffic engineering, which introduced wider metric spaces and new TLVs to further improve scalability and flexibility.
sections.plainLanguage: This builds on earlier specifications and compares itself to other ways of solving the same problem.
